bp: Imagine a committee, jury, online community, or group of agents that must choose between two outcomes while each person sees only a private clue about an underlying truth. If everyone knew the truth, the group could ask which side is actually favored by the majority under that truth. But in real voting, people do not only report clues. They also care about the final decision, and they may reason strategically: should I vote sincerely, or would my side be better off if several of us voted differently? This paper studies that problem for majority voting. Its object is not merely a tally of votes, but the relation between hidden truth, private information, preferences determined by that truth, and the ability of groups to coordinate. The practical question is when majority voting really aggregates information, rather than becoming a stage for strategic behavior.
wh: The hard part is that private information and group strategy pull in opposite directions. Majority voting is attractive because it seems to let many partial clues combine into a better collective decision. That simple story assumes each agent votes in a way that reveals what they know. But once agents understand the voting rule, they may choose votes based on how the final outcome affects them, not merely on their own signal. Previous analyses took two extremes: either agents cannot coordinate their deviations, or they can coordinate without limit. Those extremes give predictions that are too broad or too narrow, because many real groups sit between them. A few agents may talk, organize, or share strategy, while full society-wide coordination is unrealistic. The paper therefore asks how predictions change when the largest strategically coordinated coalition has size k.
naive: A smart beginner might say: count the private clues, let everyone vote for the option their clue supports, and trust the majority. If the majority of agents would favor one decision when the truth were known, the vote should find it. The failure is that votes are not neutral measurements. Each agent has preferences tied to the unobservable truth, and agents can reason about how their ballots affect the outcome. A small group may benefit from deviating together even when no single person would deviate alone. On the other hand, assuming every possible coalition can coordinate may rule out outcomes that are actually stable when only small groups can organize.
ap: The central move is to treat coordination ability as a real parameter of the voting environment instead of hiding it inside an all-or-nothing assumption. The paper asks: if no coalition of at most k agents can gain by jointly changing its behavior before private signals are realized, when does majority voting lead to the informed majority decision? That informed decision means the outcome the majority would want if the hidden ground truth were common knowledge. The method does not try to simulate every possible election one by one. It gives closed-form characterizations, meaning explicit mathematical boundaries, for two questions: whether every k-strong equilibrium reaches the informed majority decision, and whether at least one such equilibrium reaches it. The answer depends on coordination ability, the fraction of majority agents, and the information structure.
mech: The mechanism begins with a model of agents, a hidden ground truth, and private information about that truth. The hidden truth determines which decision each agent prefers, but each agent only observes a signal rather than the truth itself. The voting rule is majority voting, so the final outcome is determined by the larger side of the submitted ballots. The analysis then chooses a coordination level k. This number is the largest group size the model treats as capable of planning a joint strategic deviation. For any proposed voting behavior, the paper checks whether some group of size at most k would all expect to benefit by changing their strategy together before signals are observed. If no such group exists, the behavior is a k-strong equilibrium. The paper then compares equilibrium outcomes against the informed majority decision, the decision that would be chosen by the majority if the hidden truth were revealed to all. It solves two versions of the comparison. The first is a guarantee question: do all stable behaviors lead to the informed majority decision? The second is an existence question: is there at least one stable behavior that does so? The resulting conditions are expressed through coordination ability, majority size, and the information structure.
math: The main mathematics is game theory under uncertainty. Game theory appears because each vote is a choice made while anticipating other people's choices. Uncertainty appears because the ground truth is hidden and each agent has only private information. A Bayesian model is the bookkeeping device for this uncertainty: it describes what agents believe before the truth and signals are fully known, and how expected benefit is judged from those beliefs. The equilibrium idea is a stability test. A voting pattern is stable not because it is morally right, but because no allowed group can all improve by moving away from it together. The word k-strong adds a size limit to that test: coalitions up to k are checked, but larger coalitions are treated as beyond the environment's coordination ability. Closed-form characterization means the paper turns many possible strategic cases into explicit conditions. The surprising non-continuous, non-linear, segmental boundary for one question says that increasing coordination or changing majority size does not smoothly change what is possible overall. Small structural changes can move the voting system into a different strategic region.
dots: This paper connects to mechanism design, probability, and strategic decision-making across the conference. Like auction and allocation papers, it studies a rule that must work when participants have private information and incentives to act strategically. Like causal and uncertainty-focused papers, it separates what is actually true from what observers can infer from partial evidence. It also sits near fairness and collective decision work, because the goal is not only to predict a winner but to ask when the winner represents the decision the informed majority would choose. Its distinctive contribution is the middle layer between individual strategy and unlimited coalition power. Many systems assume users act alone or that coordinated manipulation is total. This paper argues that the size of feasible coordination is itself a structural feature, and changing that feature changes which outcomes can be trusted.
ww: The approach works because the main weakness in the naive view is not the counting rule alone; it is the missing model of coordinated incentives. If agents cannot coordinate at all, stability only has to survive one-person deviations. If any coalition can coordinate, stability must survive the strongest possible group move. Both tests can misdescribe real settings. By indexing stability by k, the analysis matches the threat model to the actual ability of agents to organize. This lets the paper distinguish outcomes that are vulnerable to small coalitions from outcomes that only fail under unrealistically large coordination. The informed majority decision becomes the reference point because it separates information aggregation from mere strategic success. A voting outcome is good in this model when the rule uses private signals well enough that the collective decision matches what the majority would favor under known truth. The closed-form conditions matter because they show exactly which combinations of coordination ability, majority fraction, and information structure make that alignment stable or at least possible.
po: The payoff is a more refined way to predict majority voting outcomes when voters are informed, interested, and only partly able to coordinate. Instead of saying majority voting always aggregates information, or that strategic behavior makes it hopeless, the paper identifies conditions under which informed majority decisions are guaranteed across all k-strong equilibria and conditions under which at least one such equilibrium exists. It also reveals that the existence boundary can be irregular rather than smooth, which warns designers not to expect simple monotone rules about coalition size or majority fraction.
limits: The result depends on the model's assumptions: agents have private information about an unobservable ground truth, that truth determines preferences, and coordination ability can be summarized by the largest coalition size k. The abstract does not prove that real groups know k, that coordination costs are uniform, or that agents share the exact information structure assumed by the model. It also reports characterizations rather than empirical evidence from actual elections. The conclusions are therefore strongest as theoretical predictions for settings that match the voting, information, and coalition assumptions.
